sections.title: The Southern Table
sections.blurb: The words a Southern menu assumes you grew up with: field peas and pot likker, hominy and hoecakes, the grapes and syrups of the region.

sections.title: Cooking Methods
sections.blurb: The verbs on the menu. What each one does to the food, how it shows on the plate, and how to tell the near neighbors apart.

sections.title: Poultry, Game & Offal
sections.blurb: Small birds, game and the organ meats: what each animal is, how rich or mild it eats, and an honest way to describe it to a nervous guest.

sections.title: Cured & Preserved Meats
sections.blurb: The charcuterie board by name: which cut, which country, salted or smoked, cooked or raw, and how each one tastes beside the others.

sections.title: Meat Cuts
sections.blurb: Where on the animal a cut comes from decides how it has to be cooked and how it eats. The steaks, the braising cuts and the ones in between.

sections.title: Fish & Shellfish
sections.blurb: The fish case: lean or rich, flaky or firm, mild or full, and where it swims. Plus the shellfish and the roes a server gets asked about.

sections.title: Mushrooms & Truffles
sections.blurb: Cultivated and wild mushrooms by texture and flavor, the names one mushroom hides behind, and what a truffle is and is not.

sections.title: Dairy & Cheese Words
sections.blurb: Butters, cultured creams, fresh cheeses and the style words on a cheese course: which milk, how it is made and how it tastes.

sections.title: Grains, Pasta & Starches
sections.blurb: Grains, corn, rice and pasta shapes: what each one is, how it eats, and the names that are easy to mix up.

sections.title: Sauces, Stocks & Dressings
sections.blurb: The mother sauces and their children, the emulsions, the stocks beneath them and the cold sauces: what goes in each and what it does on the plate.

sections.title: Preparations & Style Words
sections.blurb: Dish names that are really instructions: raw, cured, stuffed, rolled, baked under a crust, or finished in the classic French manner.

sections.title: Bread, Pastry & Cakes
sections.blurb: Doughs and batters from the bread basket to the dessert menu, and the pairs of words that sound alike and are not the same thing.

sections.title: Custards, Creams & Frozen Desserts
sections.blurb: Everything set with egg, cream, gelatin or cold: the custards, the chocolate work and the frozen desserts, told apart by what goes in them.

sections.title: Pantry, Pickles & Vinegars
sections.blurb: The jars behind the dish: vinegars and grape musts, pickles and preserves, ferments and the seasonings that finish a plate.

sections.title: Menu Language & Sourcing Words
sections.blurb: The words that are not food: how a menu is structured, what the kitchen stations are called, and what a sourcing claim does and does not mean.

cards.gist: Coarse, heavily smoked Louisiana pork sausage with garlic and cayenne
cards.guest: It's Louisiana's smoked pork sausage, coarse and garlicky with a peppery kick. It's what gives gumbo and jambalaya their deep, smoky backbone.
cards.why: Chunks of pork shoulder, not a fine grind, are seasoned with garlic, black pepper and cayenne, cased and smoked hard, often over pecan wood. It comes out firm, dark and smoky enough to season a whole pot. Think kielbasa, but coarser and hotter.
cards.pairs: Gumbo, jambalaya, red beans and rice, shrimp and grits
cards.notThis: Not tasso, its smokehouse partner, a solid spiced slab of shoulder. French andouille, its ancestor, is a tripe sausage.
cards.line: Chicken and andouille gumbo, Carolina Gold rice

cards.gist: Paprika-red pork sausage, dry-cured in Spain and sold raw in Mexico
cards.guest: It's a garlicky pork sausage stained deep red. Sliced like salami it's the cured Spanish kind, and crumbled it's the fresh Mexican kind, which is spicier.
cards.why: Two products share one word. Spanish chorizo is chopped pork cured with pimentón, the smoked paprika that gives it color and smoke, then dried until sliceable. Mexican chorizo is raw ground pork with dried chiles and vinegar, cooked loose so its red fat stains the dish.
cards.note: Ask the kitchen which kind. Cured Spanish chorizo is air-dried, not cooked, and sliced as is. Fresh Mexican chorizo is always cooked.
cards.origin: Spain and Portugal, remade in Mexico with local chiles
cards.line: Steamed clams, Spanish chorizo, white wine, grilled bread
cards.prompt: Two products share one word. Spanish __ is chopped pork cured with pimentón, the smoked paprika that gives it color and smoke, then dried until sliceable. Mexican __ is raw ground pork with dried chiles and vinegar, cooked loose so its red fat stains the dish.

cards.gist: Italian dry-cured pork neck muscle, marbled and sliced paper thin
cards.guest: It's dry-cured pork neck, sliced thin like prosciutto but with more marbling and a little more spice. Rich, tender and slightly sweet.
cards.why: The muscle running from the neck into the shoulder is salted, rubbed with pepper and spices, cased and hung to dry for months. Several small muscles meet here, so ribbons of fat run through the lean, making it richer and more seasoned than prosciutto and softer than salami.
cards.note: A dry-cured coppa is air-dried, not cooked, and is served as is in thin slices.
cards.notThis: Not prosciutto, which is the whole hind leg cured with salt alone. Coppa is a smaller, spiced, fattier muscle.
cards.line: Coppa, pickled peppers, grilled sourdough

cards.gist: American pork leg, dry-salted, often smoked, then aged for months
cards.guest: It's the South's answer to prosciutto, a pork leg packed in salt and aged for months. It's salty, deep and a little funky, so a thin slice goes a long way.
cards.why: A whole pork leg is packed in dry salt, often with sugar, usually smoked over hickory, then hung through a summer or longer. It loses water and concentrates, so it eats firm, intensely salty and savory. City ham is brined instead, so it stays moist and mild.
cards.note: Served two ways: shaved uncooked like prosciutto, or sliced thicker and pan-fried. Ask the kitchen which.
cards.pairs: Biscuits, red-eye gravy, grits, melon, pickles
cards.line: Shaved country ham, buttermilk biscuits, sorghum butter
cards.prompt: A whole pork leg is packed in dry salt, often with sugar, usually smoked over hickory, then hung through a summer or longer. It loses water and concentrates, so it eats firm, intensely salty and savory. City __ is brined instead, so it stays moist and mild.

cards.gist: Italian cured pork jowl, unsmoked, richer and fattier than belly
cards.guest: It's cured pork jowl, the fatty cheek, like an unsmoked Italian bacon with richer, silkier fat. It's the classic pork in carbonara and amatriciana.
cards.why: The jowl is rubbed with salt, black pepper and sometimes herbs, then hung to dry for weeks. It is mostly fat with streaks of lean, and that fat is firmer and more flavorful than belly fat. In a pan it renders into crisp pieces and a savory fat that becomes the sauce.
cards.note: Nearly always cooked: diced and rendered until crisp, not sliced for a board.
cards.notThis: Not pancetta, which is cured belly, leaner and milder, and not bacon, which is smoked belly. This is the jowl.
cards.line: Bucatini all'amatriciana, guanciale, pecorino

cards.gist: Italian cured pork back fat, aged with salt and herbs, shaved thin
cards.guest: It's pure pork back fat cured with salt, rosemary and garlic until it's silky and sweet. Shaved thin over warm toast, it melts like butter.
cards.why: Thick slabs of fat from the pig's back are layered with sea salt, rosemary, garlic and spices and cured for months, traditionally in marble tubs in Colonnata, Tuscany. The cure firms and perfumes it, so a thin slice turns translucent and melts on anything warm.
cards.note: Served uncooked in paper-thin slices, best laid on something warm so it softens.
cards.notThis: Not lard, the rendered cooking fat. Lardo is a cured solid slab, sliced and eaten like other cured meats.
cards.line: Grilled sourdough, lardo, rosemary, sea salt

cards.gist: Spanish air-dried whole pork loin, lean, rubbed with smoked paprika
cards.guest: It's Spanish cured pork loin, air-dried with smoked paprika and garlic. It's as lean as cured pork gets, clean, meaty and gently smoky.
cards.why: The whole loin, the long lean muscle along the back, is trimmed, rubbed with salt, pimentón and garlic, cased and dried for two months or more. With almost no fat it slices rosy and eats firm and meaty. From ibérico pigs it shows fine marbling and a nutty depth.
cards.note: Air-dried, not cooked, and served as is in thin slices.
cards.origin: Spain; lomo is Spanish for loin
cards.notThis: Not tenderloin. Lomo is the loin, the big muscle along the back. On a Latin American menu it can mean fresh beef.
cards.line: Lomo ibérico, marcona almonds, olive oil

cards.gist: Italian pork belly cured with salt and spice, air-dried, not smoked
cards.guest: It's Italian bacon without the smoke, pork belly cured with salt, pepper and spices. It tastes cleaner and sweeter than American bacon, all pork and spice.
cards.why: Same cut as bacon, the belly, but salt-cured with pepper, garlic and spices such as juniper or nutmeg, then air-dried for weeks instead of smoked. It comes as a flat slab for dicing or a rolled spiral for slicing. Without smoke, the sweet pork and spice come through.
cards.note: Usually diced and cooked crisp. Thin-sliced rolled pancetta may be served uncooked, so ask the kitchen.
cards.notThis: Not bacon, which is smoked, and not guanciale, which is the jowl. Pancetta is unsmoked belly.
cards.line: Brussels sprouts, crisp pancetta, aged balsamic

cards.gist: Brined beef, crusted in pepper and coriander, smoked, then steamed
cards.guest: It's beef cured like corned beef, then crusted in cracked pepper and coriander, smoked and steamed until tender. Peppery, smoky and rich.
cards.why: Brisket, or the fattier navel cut beside it, sits in brine for days, which seasons it through and keeps it rosy. Then a pepper and coriander rub, smoke, and a long steam that melts the tough tissue. Think corned beef with a crust and a smoky edge.
cards.note: Fully cooked. The pink color comes from the cure, not from doneness, so there is no temperature to ask for.
cards.notThis: Not corned beef, which shares the brine but is simmered, with no pepper crust and no smoke.
cards.line: House pastrami, rye, whole grain mustard, pickles

cards.gist: Ground meat, fat, often liver, baked, chilled, spread on toast
cards.guest: It's a French meat spread, usually pork and liver, baked and chilled. It can be silky or coarse, and it's rich, so a little on toast goes a long way.
cards.why: Meat, fat and usually some liver are ground with salt, spice and often brandy, packed into a mold and baked gently in a water bath. Chilled, it sets firm enough to slice. Liver gives the deep mineral richness, and fat makes it spread.
cards.note: Served cold. Liver versions are often left pink inside, so ask the kitchen how theirs is cooked.
cards.notThis: Not rillettes, which are shredded, and not foie gras, fattened duck or goose liver. A terrine is the same family, named for its mold.
cards.line: Country pâté, cornichons, Dijon, grilled sourdough

cards.gist: Italian pork leg, salted, air-dried a year or more, shaved thin
cards.guest: It's Italian ham, salted and air-dried for a year or more, never cooked or smoked. Sliced paper-thin, it's silky, a little sweet, and melts on your tongue.
cards.why: A whole hind leg is rubbed with sea salt, then hung in moving air for a year or longer. It slowly loses water while the meat's own enzymes build sweet, nutty flavor. Cut thin, the fat melts on contact. It is sweeter and softer than Spanish ham.
cards.note: Served raw, as cured. Heat turns it salty and tough, so it goes on hot dishes last.
cards.pairs: Melon, figs, burrata, arugula, breadsticks
cards.notThis: Not speck, the same leg lightly smoked, not pancetta, cured belly for cooking, and not jamón ibérico, Spain's longer-aged ham.
cards.line: Prosciutto di Parma, compressed melon, basil

cards.gist: Meat cooked slowly in its own fat, then shredded into a rich spread
cards.guest: Think pulled pork, but French and spreadable. The meat cooks for hours in its own fat until it falls apart, then it's packed in a jar and served with toast.
cards.why: Pork, duck or rabbit is salted and simmered very gently in fat until it collapses, then shredded, stirred with some of that fat and sealed in a jar under a fat cap. It is soft and stringy, not smooth, and it tastes milder than liver-rich pâté.
cards.note: Served cool, not fridge-cold, so the fat softens and spreads. The pale layer of fat on top is normal.
cards.notThis: Not pâté, which is ground and baked, usually with liver. Not confit, which is served whole, not shredded.
cards.line: Pork rillettes, grilled bread, cornichons, mustard

cards.gist: Boned pork leg cured with juniper, lightly cold smoked, then aged
cards.guest: It's a smoked cousin of prosciutto from the Italian Alps, cured with juniper and mountain herbs. It's a bit firmer, with a gentle smoky finish.
cards.why: Alto Adige sits on the Austrian border, and its ham borrows from both sides: dry cured like prosciutto, then cold smoked over beechwood. The leg is rubbed with salt, juniper, bay and pepper and aged about five months. Boned, flat and smoked, it eats firmer than prosciutto.
cards.note: Served raw, as cured. Cold smoke flavors it but does not cook it.
cards.pairs: Rye bread, pickles, horseradish, apples, mountain cheeses
cards.notThis: Not prosciutto, which is never smoked. In German the word just means bacon, so on an Austrian menu it may be bacon.
cards.line: Speck, shaved apple, horseradish cream, rye crisps

cards.gist: Cajun pork shoulder, cured, crusted in cayenne and garlic, smoked
cards.guest: It's Cajun smoked pork, rubbed with cayenne and garlic. Spicy, salty and very smoky, so the kitchen dices it small to season a dish, the way you'd use bacon.
cards.why: Called a ham, but it is not leg meat. Pork shoulder is cut into slabs, briefly cured, packed in a cayenne, garlic and paprika rub and hot smoked until cooked through. Too intense to eat by the slice, it goes into gumbo, jambalaya, beans, grits and cream sauces.
cards.origin: South Louisiana, the name likely from Spanish tasajo, dried meat
cards.notThis: Not andouille, its smokehouse partner, which is a sausage in a casing. This is a solid piece of shoulder.
cards.line: Shrimp and grits, tasso ham gravy, scallions

cards.gist: French craft of salting, smoking and preserving meat, mostly pork
cards.guest: It's the French word for cured and prepared meats, like ham, salami and pâté. A board is a selection made for sharing, with pickles, mustard and bread.
cards.why: The word comes from the French for cooked flesh and named the pork butcher's shop. Before refrigeration, salting, drying, smoking and cooking in fat were how meat lasted the winter. A good board contrasts textures: a silky ham, a firm salami, something spreadable.
cards.note: Dry-cured ham, salami and bresaola are served raw, as cured.
cards.notThis: Not a cheese board. Italy calls the same craft salumi, and salami is only one kind of it.
cards.line: Charcuterie board, house pickles, mustard, grilled bread

cards.gist: Lean beef round, salted with wine and spice, air-dried deep red
cards.guest: It's very lean air-dried beef from the Italian Alps. Deep red, tender and a little sweet, usually dressed with olive oil and lemon.
cards.why: A single muscle from the beef round is trimmed of all fat, salted with wine, pepper, juniper and garlic, then hung to dry for a month or two in the Valtellina valley of Lombardy. With almost no fat it eats dense and clean, like a beefy prosciutto.
cards.note: Served raw, sliced very thin. Once cut it dries and darkens quickly, so it is sliced to order.
cards.notThis: Not carpaccio, which is fresh raw beef. This is cured and dried for weeks, so it is firmer and saltier.
cards.line: Bresaola, arugula, lemon, shaved Parmesan

cards.gist: Coarse-cut pressed dry salami of southern Italy, often hot with chili
cards.guest: It's a rustic dry salami from southern Italy, chopped coarse so you get real pieces of pork in every slice. Meatier and bolder than everyday salami.
cards.why: Lean pork and firm fat are chopped, not finely ground, seasoned with salt, pepper and often Calabrian chili, and cased. Pressed under weights for the first days, then hung to dry for weeks, it eats dense, chewy and tangy, like a rougher Genoa salami.
cards.note: Dry-cured, never cooked. Sold hot or sweet: sweet means mild, not sugary. Know which is on the board.
cards.origin: Calabria and Basilicata, Italy; from soppressare, to press down
cards.line: Hot soppressata, aged provolone, marinated olives

cards.gist: Soft, fiery Calabrian pork salami that spreads like butter
cards.guest: It's a spicy, spreadable salami from Calabria in southern Italy. Think of a soft, smoky chili and pork spread that melts into warm bread.
cards.why: Fatty pork is ground very fine with a huge share of Calabrian chili, as much as a third by weight, then stuffed in a casing, lightly smoked and fermented. So much fat and chili keeps it from ever firming up, so it stays a brick-red paste: rich, tangy, smoky and hot.
cards.note: Cured and fermented, never cooked. Often served as it is, spread on bread.
cards.origin: Spilinga, Calabria; the name likely comes from the French andouille
cards.pairs: Grilled bread, pizza, pasta sauces, eggs, burrata, honey
cards.line: Grilled sourdough, 'nduja, burrata, honey

cards.gist: Long-aged dry ham from Spain's native black pigs, carved paper-thin
cards.guest: It's Spain's great cured ham, from black Iberian pigs and aged for years. It's nutty and a little sweet, and the fat melts on your tongue.
cards.why: The Iberian pig stores fat inside the muscle, and the top grade, bellota, fattens on acorns in oak pasture. Legs are salted, then hung 2 to 4 years. That fat is soft enough to melt at room temperature, so slices turn glossy, nutty and deeper than prosciutto.
cards.note: Served uncooked, at room temperature. White specks are crystals from long aging, not a flaw.
cards.notThis: Not prosciutto, which is Italian, from white pigs, and milder. Spain's everyday serrano also comes from white pigs.
cards.line: Hand-carved jamón ibérico de bellota, pan con tomate

cards.gist: Pork belly cured with salt and sugar, smoked, then sliced to crisp
cards.guest: It's pork belly cured with salt and a little sugar, then smoked over wood. Cooked until the fat crisps, it's salty, smoky and a touch sweet.
cards.why: Belly is layered fat and lean. About a week in salt, sugar and curing salt firms it and keeps the lean rosy, then hickory or applewood smoke adds the signature flavor. In the pan the fat renders out and the strips crisp. Lardons are short batons cut from the slab.
cards.note: Bacon labeled uncured is still cured, with celery powder standing in for curing salt.
cards.notThis: Not pancetta, the same belly cured but usually not smoked. Pork belly on a menu is the fresh cut, not cured.
cards.line: Thick-cut applewood bacon, maple, black pepper

cards.gist: Loaf of seasoned chopped meats baked in a mold, chilled and sliced
cards.guest: It's a French country-style meat loaf, served cold in slices. Think of a coarse, rich pâté you eat with a fork, with mustard and pickles.
cards.why: Seasoned chopped pork, liver and fat, often with brandy, are packed into a deep rectangular mold, also called a terrine, and baked gently in a water bath. Pressed and chilled overnight, it slices clean, showing a mosaic of meat, fat and garnish.
cards.note: Not every terrine is pork. Vegetables, fish or foie gras are layered the same way.
cards.notThis: Not quite pâté, which names the mixture and is often smooth and spreadable. A terrine is named for its mold and served sliced.
cards.line: Country pork terrine, cornichons, grain mustard, toast
cards.prompt: Seasoned chopped pork, liver and fat, often with brandy, are packed into a deep rectangular mold, also called a __, and baked gently in a water bath. Pressed and chilled overnight, it slices clean, showing a mosaic of meat, fat and garnish.

cards.gist: Brisket cured in spiced salt brine, then simmered until fork-tender
cards.guest: It's beef brisket cured for days in a salty, spiced brine, then simmered until it's tender. It's pink, salty and gently spiced, the heart of a Reuben.
cards.why: Brisket sits 5 to 10 days in a brine of salt, sugar, curing salt and pickling spices such as bay, mustard seed and coriander. The cure keeps it pink, and long simmering softens the tough cut. Corn is an old word for coarse grains of salt.
cards.note: Pink here comes from the curing salt and does not mean undercooked.
cards.notThis: Not pastrami, which starts with the same kind of cure but is then rubbed in pepper and coriander and smoked.
cards.line: House corned beef Reuben, sauerkraut, Swiss, rye

cards.gist: Heavily marbled crescent of beef that wraps the outside of a rib steak
cards.guest: It's the outer strip of a ribeye, the part most people save for the last bite. You get ribeye richness with the softness of a filet.
cards.why: A ribeye is the round eye plus a thin crescent curving over it. That crescent, the spinalis, has the most marbling on the steak and a loose, open grain, so it eats softer and richer than the eye. One animal yields very little, hence the price.
cards.note: Thin, so it cooks fast. The marbling needs heat to melt, and most kitchens send it medium rare.
cards.notThis: Not coulotte, the leaner sirloin cap from the back end. Calotte and coulotte sound alike on a menu.
cards.line: Grilled ribeye cap, charred onion, bordelaise
cards.prompt: A __ is the round eye plus a thin crescent curving over it. That crescent, the __, has the most marbling on the steak and a loose, open grain, so it eats softer and richer than the eye. One animal yields very little, hence the price.

cards.gist: Hard-working chewing muscle of the face, braised until spoon-soft
cards.guest: It's the cheek muscle, braised for hours until it cuts with a spoon. Think of the richest pot roast you've had, silkier and deeper in flavor.
cards.why: An animal chews all day, so this muscle is dense with connective tissue and tough as leather cooked fast. Braised low for three hours or more, that tissue melts into gelatin, making the meat sticky and silky and the braising liquid a glossy sauce.
cards.note: Always slow cooked through, so there is no temperature to ask the guest for.
cards.pairs: Red wine braise, polenta, mashed potato, root vegetables
cards.line: Braised beef cheek, soft polenta, red wine jus

cards.gist: One thick cut of beef from the diaphragm, loose-grained and deeply mineral
cards.guest: It's the butcher's steak, the one they used to keep for themselves. Loose grain, deep beef flavor, and usually served sliced.
cards.why: It hangs between the last rib and the loin, the thick central pillar of the diaphragm, one per animal. Bearing no weight, it stays fairly soft, but a coarse grain and rich blood supply give it a mineral flavor bolder than strip or filet. It is sliced across the grain.
cards.note: Best at medium rare. Past medium it tightens and turns chewy, so steer well-done guests elsewhere.
cards.notThis: Not skirt steak, the long thin belt of diaphragm beside it. Hanger is one short, thick piece.
cards.line: Grilled hanger steak, chimichurri, fries

cards.gist: Bony lower leg joint of a pig, usually smoked and simmered to flavor a pot
cards.guest: It's the smoked lower joint of the pork leg. It simmers in the pot for hours and gives the whole dish a deep, smoky pork flavor.
cards.why: The hock is where the leg meets the foot: mostly skin, tendon and bone with a little meat, usually cured and smoked like ham. Simmered for hours, the skin and tendon melt into gelatin that gives body to beans, greens and soups, and the smoke and salt season the pot.
cards.note: A hock often seasons a dish without showing on the plate. Mention the pork when a guest asks what is in it.
cards.pairs: Collard greens, split pea soup, white beans, black-eyed peas
cards.line: White beans, smoked ham hock, cornbread
cards.prompt: The __ is where the leg meets the foot: mostly skin, tendon and bone with a little meat, usually cured and smoked like __. Simmered for hours, the skin and tendon melt into gelatin that gives body to beans, greens and soups, and the smoke and salt season the pot.

cards.gist: Upper rib beef steak, the most marbled of the classic steakhouse cuts
cards.guest: It's the richest of the classic steaks, cut from the rib and marbled all the way through. For big beef flavor and a juicy bite, this is the one.
cards.why: It comes from high on the back over the ribs, a muscle that does little work, so it is soft and threaded with fat that melts and bastes the meat from inside. It is fattier and bolder than a strip and far richer than a filet. Roasted whole, the same cut is prime rib.
cards.note: Medium rare to medium suits it better than rare, where the fat can stay waxy.
cards.pairs: Creamed spinach, baked potato, red wine sauce, Cabernet
cards.line: 16 oz bone-in ribeye, roasted garlic butter

cards.gist: Hard-working cut above the front leg that shreds after hours of low heat
cards.guest: Shoulder is the cut made for slow cooking. After hours of low heat it pulls apart with a fork and has more flavor than any of the lean cuts.
cards.why: The front legs carry most of an animal's weight, so the shoulder is dense with connective tissue and seamed with fat, and chewy if cooked fast. Braised, smoked or slow roasted for hours, that tissue melts and the meat shreds. It is pulled pork and carnitas on a pig, pot roast on a steer.
cards.notThis: Pork butt, or Boston butt, is the upper shoulder, not the rear of the pig. The rear leg is the ham.
cards.line: Slow-roasted lamb shoulder, white beans, salsa verde
cards.prompt: The front legs carry most of an animal's weight, so the __ is dense with connective tissue and seamed with fat, and chewy if cooked fast. Braised, smoked or slow roasted for hours, that tissue melts and the meat shreds. It is pulled pork and carnitas on a pig, pot roast on a steer.

cards.gist: Fatty beef on stubby bones from low on the chest, braised until it yields
cards.guest: Short rib is thick, well-marbled beef braised for hours until it falls off the bone. Rich and soft, like pot roast turned all the way up.
cards.why: It comes from the lower rib cage, in the chuck and plate, where the meat is heavily marbled and layered with connective tissue. A long braise melts both, so the beef holds its shape but gives to a fork. Sawn thin across the bones, the same cut is grilled fast for Korean barbecue.
cards.note: Braised short rib is cooked through. There is no temperature to ask the guest for.
cards.pairs: Red wine sauce, mashed potato, polenta, horseradish
cards.line: Red wine braised short rib, potato puree, glazed carrots
cards.prompt: It comes from the lower __ cage, in the chuck and plate, where the meat is heavily marbled and layered with connective tissue. A long braise melts both, so the beef holds its shape but gives to a fork. Sawn thin across the bones, the same cut is grilled fast for Korean barbecue.

cards.gist: Small tapered muscle under the spine, the softest, mildest steak cut
cards.guest: Tenderloin is the most tender cut on the animal, the one filet mignon comes from. Lean, mild and so soft you barely need the knife.
cards.why: A long, narrow muscle under the backbone that does almost no work, it has very little connective tissue and cuts like butter. The trade is flavor: lean, with little marbling, it tastes milder than a ribeye or strip, so it often comes with a sauce, a butter or a bacon wrap.
cards.note: Beef filet dries out past medium, so most kitchens suggest rare to medium rare. Pork tenderloin is always cooked further.
cards.pairs: Bearnaise, peppercorn sauce, red wine sauce, mushrooms
cards.line: 8 oz beef tenderloin, bearnaise, pommes puree

cards.gist: Fresh, uncured slab from the underside of the pig, layered fat and lean
cards.guest: It's the same cut as bacon, only fresh. It's very rich, cooked slowly until spoon tender, then crisped on the outside.
cards.why: The boneless underside of the pig, in alternating layers of fat and lean. Slow cooking melts the fat and softens the meat, then high heat crisps the surface or the skin. Rich like short rib but softer and sweeter, so portions are small and come with something sharp.
cards.pairs: Pickles, apples, mustard, bitter greens, soy and ginger glazes
cards.notThis: Not bacon, which is this cut cured and smoked, nor pancetta, cured and not smoked. Belly on a menu is fresh meat.
cards.line: Crispy pork belly, apple mostarda, mustard greens

cards.gist: Short loin steak with a firm, tight bite and a band of fat down one edge
cards.guest: It's the classic steakhouse steak, with a firmer bite and beefier flavor than filet. It's a little leaner than a ribeye, with an edge of fat that crisps on the grill.
cards.why: Cut from the short loin, along the back just behind the ribs. It is the same long back muscle as the ribeye, only further back, where it carries less marbling. That muscle does little work, so it stays tender, with a tight grain and a clean chew.
cards.origin: Named for New York steakhouses, where it became the house cut
cards.pairs: Peppercorn sauce, compound butter, creamed spinach, fries
cards.line: 14 oz New York strip, bone marrow butter, watercress

cards.gist: One large steak holding two: strip on one side, tenderloin on the other
cards.guest: It's two steaks on one T-shaped bone, a New York strip on one side and filet on the other. The porterhouse is the bigger cut, with more filet.
cards.why: Both are sawn across the short loin, so each slice catches the strip above the bone and the tenderloin below it. The tenderloin tapers toward the front, so rear steaks, with a wide filet, are porterhouses and forward ones are T-bones. USDA sets the line at 1.25 inches of filet.
cards.note: The filet side cooks faster than the strip side, so the two halves rarely land at the same doneness.
cards.pairs: Creamed spinach, hash browns, a big red wine
cards.line: Porterhouse for two, 32 oz, roasted garlic, sea salt
cards.prompt: Both are sawn across the short loin, so each slice catches the strip above the __ and the tenderloin below it. The tenderloin tapers toward the front, so rear steaks, with a wide filet, are __ and forward ones are T-__. USDA sets the line at 1.25 inches of filet.

cards.gist: Wide, lean sheet of beef from the lower abdomen with a long grain
cards.guest: A lean, flat steak with big beefy flavor, cooked hot and fast and sliced thin across the grain, so it's tender with a little chew.
cards.why: One flat abdominal muscle from just ahead of the back legs. It works constantly, so it is lean and full of flavor, with long fibers running its whole length. Sliced thin across them it is tender, along them stringy.
cards.note: Best at medium rare to medium. With so little fat it dries out and toughens past that.
cards.pairs: Chimichurri, citrus or soy marinades, steak salads
cards.notThis: Not skirt, a longer, fattier ribbon from under the ribs, nor bavette, the looser-grained sirloin flap.
cards.line: Grilled flank steak, chimichurri, charred onions

cards.gist: Long, thin ribbon of beef from under the ribs, loose grained, well marbled
cards.guest: A long, thin steak with a loose grain and rich marbling, so it's intensely beefy. It's the classic for carne asada.
cards.why: The outside skirt is the diaphragm and the inside skirt lies beside it, both from the plate. A thin belt with coarse fibers running across its width and more fat than flank, it soaks up marinade and chars fast. It wants fierce heat, then slicing across the grain.
cards.note: Best at medium rare to medium. It is so thin that it toughens quickly past that.
cards.origin: Fajitas take their name from it: faja is Spanish for belt
cards.notThis: Not flank, wider and leaner, nor hanger, short and thick, nor bavette, the thicker sirloin flap.
cards.line: Skirt steak carne asada, salsa verde, grilled scallions
cards.prompt: The outside __ is the diaphragm and the inside __ lies beside it, both from the plate. A thin belt with coarse fibers running across its width and more fat than flank, it soaks up marinade and chars fast. It wants fierce heat, then slicing across the grain.

cards.gist: Loose, open-grained bottom sirloin steak, a French bistro favorite
cards.guest: A French bistro steak from the sirloin, next to the flank. Loose, juicy grain and deep beefy flavor, like skirt but thicker and more tender.
cards.why: It is the sirloin flap, a thin muscle where the bottom sirloin meets the flank. Its coarse, open fibers have good marbling between them, so it holds marinade and sauce, takes a hard sear and stays juicy.
cards.note: Best at medium rare, sliced across the grain. Past medium it turns chewy.
cards.origin: French for bib, bistro shorthand for flat belly-side steaks
cards.notThis: Not flank or skirt, though in France the word covers several flat cuts. Here it is sirloin flap, looser and more marbled than flank.
cards.line: Bavette steak, shallot butter, frites

cards.gist: Chuck steak with its tough center gristle cut out, nearly as tender as filet
cards.guest: Flat iron is a shoulder steak, second only to filet for tenderness. It has more marbling than filet, so it tastes beefier.
cards.why: It is the top blade muscle from the shoulder, or chuck. A thick seam of gristle runs through its middle, which kept it off menus until meat scientists in Nebraska and Florida showed, around 2002, how to cut it out, leaving two flat, well-marbled steaks.
cards.origin: Named for its shape, like an old flat clothes iron
cards.pairs: Salsa verde, chimichurri, fries, bistro salads
cards.line: Flat iron steak, salsa verde, crispy potatoes
cards.prompt: It is the top blade muscle from the shoulder, or chuck. A thick seam of gristle runs through its middle, which kept it off menus until meat scientists in Nebraska and Florida showed, around 2002, how to cut it out, leaving two __, well-marbled __.

cards.gist: Tough chest muscle of beef that turns tender only after hours of slow heat
cards.guest: Beef from the chest, cooked slowly for hours until tender and juicy, with deep beefy flavor and a rich, melting edge of fat.
cards.why: The chest muscles carry much of the steer's weight, so they are dense with connective tissue. Hours of low heat, in smoke or a braise, melt it into gelatin for a moist, silky slice. The flat is the lean half and the point the fatty half. Cured, it becomes corned beef and, often, pastrami.
cards.note: Sliced across the grain. Smoked brisket often shows a pink ring under the crust: the smoke ring, and it is normal.
cards.pairs: Pickles, raw onion and white bread, or carrots and onions in a braise
cards.line: Smoked brisket, house pickles, white bread, mustard slaw

cards.gist: Rounds of beef tail, braised until the meat slips off the bone
cards.guest: Oxtail is the tail of the steer, cut into thick rounds and braised for hours until it falls off the bone. It's rich, sticky and deeply beefy.
cards.why: The tail is mostly bone, cartilage and small pockets of hard-working muscle, so it is loaded with collagen. Hours of slow, wet heat melt that into gelatin, giving silky meat and a glossy, sticky sauce. Think short rib, only deeper and more gelatinous.
cards.note: Usually served on the bone, so tell guests to expect small bones.
cards.origin: Once the tail of an ox, now of any beef cattle
cards.pairs: Butter beans, rice and peas, polenta, mashed potato
cards.line: Braised oxtail, butter beans, rice and peas

cards.gist: The lower leg, all sinew around a marrow bone, braised until spoon-tender
cards.guest: Shank is the lower leg of lamb or veal, braised for hours until it's spoon-tender and slides off the bone. The sauce is made from its own rich juices.
cards.why: The lower leg carries the animal all day, so the meat is lean, tough and laced with sinew. Hours of gentle braising melt that sinew into gelatin, giving moist shreds and a sticky sauce. Lamb comes whole on the bone. Veal is often cross-cut around its marrow bone.
cards.note: A whole lamb shank is a big portion on a long bone. The marrow in a cross-cut piece is meant to be eaten.
cards.origin: Sold as lamb, veal, beef or pork; cross-cut veal shank is Italy's osso buco
cards.pairs: Polenta, saffron risotto, white beans, mashed potato
cards.line: Braised lamb shank, creamy polenta, rosemary jus

cards.gist: The triangular cap of the top sirloin, grilled under its own fat
cards.guest: Coulotte is the cap of the top sirloin, a juicy, beefy steak cooked under its own fat so it bastes itself. In Brazil it's picanha, the star of the steakhouse.
cards.why: One triangular muscle on top of the sirloin, under a thick layer of fat. It does moderate work, so it is tender enough to grill or roast but beefier than the loin steaks. Sliced across the grain it eats like a leaner, firmer strip.
cards.note: Best at medium rare to medium, with the fat cap left on.
cards.origin: French culotte, a rump cut; Brazil's picanha, said pee-KAHN-yah
cards.notThis: Not the ribeye cap, which comes from the rib and is far richer. This one sits on the sirloin, by the hip.
cards.line: Grilled coulotte steak, chimichurri, charred onion

cards.gist: The rib section of a young sheep, roasted whole and carved into chops
cards.guest: Rack of lamb is the rib section, roasted whole and carved into chops on the bone. It's the most tender, mild cut of lamb, the ribeye of the animal.
cards.why: Seven or eight ribs with the eye of loin meat attached, a muscle along the back that barely works, so it is fine-grained and tender. The bones are often frenched, meaning scraped clean for looks. It is roasted fast and hot, then cut into single or double chops.
cards.note: Best at medium rare, rosy through the middle. Past medium the small eye of meat dries out quickly.
cards.pairs: Mustard and herb crust, mint, rosemary, garlic
cards.line: Herb-crusted rack of lamb, mint salsa verde, potato gratin

cards.gist: A thick slice across the hog's loin, usually on the bone, seared or grilled
cards.guest: A pork chop is a thick cut from the loin, the pig's answer to a bone-in strip or ribeye. Done right, it's seared outside and juicy in the middle.
cards.why: Chops are sliced across the loin, the long muscle down the pig's back. It does little work, so it is tender, but it is lean and dries out fast. Kitchens fight that with thick cuts, the bone left in, a brine and a rest. Rib chops carry more fat than center-cut loin chops.
cards.note: Many kitchens now cook it to a blush of pink, 63 C (145 F) plus a rest, so ask the chef how ours is cooked.
cards.pairs: Apples, mustard, sage, cabbage, cider sauce
cards.line: Brined bone-in pork chop, roasted apples, mustard jus
cards.prompt: __ are sliced across the loin, the long muscle down the pig's back. It does little work, so it is tender, but it is lean and dries out fast. Kitchens fight that with thick cuts, the bone left in, a brine and a rest. Rib __ carry more fat than center-cut loin __.

cards.gist: Beef from Japanese cattle breeds prized for dense, fine marbling
cards.guest: Wagyu is beef from Japanese cattle breeds famous for marbling. The fat runs all through the meat, so it's buttery, tender and so rich that a little goes a long way.
cards.why: These breeds are genetically inclined to store fat inside the muscle, not just around it, and are fed far longer than other cattle. That fat melts at a lower temperature than other beef fat, so it goes buttery in the mouth. Japan's top grade is A5. American versions are usually crossed with Angus.
cards.note: Japanese A5 is usually sold by the ounce, seared quickly and served in small portions.
cards.origin: Japanese: wa means Japanese and gyu means cattle
cards.notThis: Not the same as Kobe, one regional brand of it from Hyogo. All Kobe is Wagyu, but very little Wagyu is Kobe.
cards.line: A5 Wagyu strip, sea salt, fresh wasabi

cards.gist: Cold-water cousin of salmon and trout with pink, moderately rich flesh
cards.guest: It's a cold-water fish from the salmon family, and it eats right between salmon and trout. Rich but mild, with a fine flake and a thin skin that crisps.
cards.why: A member of the salmon family from icy northern lakes and coasts, now mostly farmed in cold tanks. Its fat sits between trout and salmon, so the pink to red flesh stays moist and fine-flaked, with a cleaner, milder flavor than salmon.
cards.note: Nearly all of it is farmed, mostly in Iceland and Canada. The thin skin crisps well and is meant to be eaten.
cards.notThis: Not salmon or trout, though kin to both. It is milder and finer than salmon, and richer than trout.
cards.line: Crispy-skin arctic char, fennel, citrus beurre blanc

cards.gist: Finger-long freshwater crustacean, a tiny lobster eaten for its tail
cards.guest: They're freshwater shellfish that look like tiny lobsters, a Louisiana staple. The tail meat is sweet and tender, somewhere between shrimp and lobster.
cards.why: A freshwater crustacean from Louisiana's swamps and rice ponds, built like a lobster about a finger long. Only the tail holds real meat, sweet and tender, while the fat in the head carries the flavor, so whole ones are boiled in spice and peeled by hand.
cards.note: Live season runs roughly late winter to early summer. Outside it, most kitchens cook with frozen peeled tail meat.
cards.pairs: Boils with corn, potato and sausage; étouffée over rice
cards.line: Crawfish étouffée, Carolina Gold rice, scallion

cards.gist: Wing of a ray, its sweet white flesh pulling apart in long strands
cards.guest: It's the wing of a ray, a cousin of the stingray. The meat is sweet and mild, a little like scallop or crab, and it pulls away in long tender strands.
cards.why: Skates are rays, with a skeleton of cartilage instead of bone. Only the wings are eaten: a fan of long muscle strands over a sheet of soft cartilage, so the flesh comes away in ribbons, not flakes. It is lean, sweet and mild, and takes well to a hot pan.
cards.note: No pin bones. A bone-in wing has a flat sheet of soft cartilage in the middle, and the meat slides off it with a fork.
cards.pairs: Black butter, capers, parsley and vinegar, the French classic, or brown butter and lemon
cards.line: Pan-roasted skate wing, brown butter, capers, lemon

cards.gist: Small, thin flatfish with lean, delicate, mild and sweet fillets
cards.guest: It's a small flatfish, lean and very delicate, with a mild, sweet flavor. If you like sole, it eats the same way, light and fine-flaked.
cards.why: A flatfish that lies on the seabed with both eyes on its upper side, left or right depending on the species. Little fat and thin fillets give a fine, soft texture and a mild, sweet taste. Fluke is summer flounder, and many American soles are flounders too. It cooks in minutes.
cards.note: Fluke is often served raw, sliced thin as crudo or sashimi.
cards.notThis: Not halibut, its giant cousin. Halibut comes as thick, firm portions, and flounder as thin, soft fillets or a whole fish.
cards.line: Pan-fried flounder, lemon, parsley, brown butter

cards.gist: Warm-water reef fish with lean, firm white meat in big chunky flakes
cards.guest: It's a mild white fish from the Gulf and the South Atlantic. The meat is firm and sweet with big, moist flakes, so it holds up to the grill or the fryer.
cards.why: A heavy-bodied reef fish of the sea bass family, caught off Florida, the Gulf and the Carolinas. It is lean but holds moisture well, and thick fillets break into large, firm flakes. The flavor is mild and faintly sweet, close to sea bass.
cards.notThis: Not snapper, the other Southern reef fish. Snapper fillets are thinner and finer-flaked, and grouper is chunkier and firmer.
cards.line: Blackened grouper sandwich, lettuce, tomato, tartar sauce

cards.gist: The largest flatfish, cut into thick, firm, snow-white lean portions
cards.guest: It's a big cold-water flatfish with thick, snow-white meat. Firm, clean and mildly sweet, the fish for someone who wants nothing fishy.
cards.why: The giant of the flatfish, a right-eyed flounder that can outweigh a person, from the cold North Pacific and North Atlantic. Its size gives thick portions with a firm, large flake. With very little fat, it tastes clean and mild and leans on sauce for richness.
cards.note: So lean it dries out fast. Kitchens pull it just as it turns opaque, and it is a poor choice for well done.
cards.origin: Middle English haly butte, holy flatfish, eaten on feast days
cards.notThis: Not flounder, a small flatfish sold in thin fillets, or turbot, which is richer and more gelatinous.
cards.line: Pan-roasted halibut, spring peas, beurre blanc

cards.gist: Blue-black bivalve with soft, sweet meat, steamed open in its own broth
cards.guest: They're shellfish in blue-black shells, steamed until they pop open. The meat is soft and sweet, milder than a clam, and the broth is made for dipping bread.
cards.why: A bivalve farmed in clusters on ropes, which keeps sand out. Steamed a few minutes with wine, garlic and shallot, the shells open and release their own liquor, which becomes the broth. The meat is plump and soft, sweeter and less briny than clam or oyster.
cards.note: A mussel still shut after steaming should be left in the bowl, not pried open. Orange or cream meat is only male or female.
cards.notThis: Not clams. Mussels have thin, blue-black teardrop shells and soft meat. Clams are rounder, paler and chewier.
cards.line: Steamed mussels, white wine, garlic, grilled bread

cards.gist: Rough-shelled bivalve, often eaten raw, that tastes of its home water
cards.guest: They're shellfish, and on the half shell they're shucked to order and eaten raw. A cold, silky bite of clean ocean, some brinier, some sweeter.
cards.why: A bivalve that filters the water it grows in, so each bay gives its own flavor, the way a vineyard does for wine. East Coast ones run briny and firm, West Coast ones sweeter and creamier, with a cucumber or melon note.
cards.note: On the half shell they come raw and alive on ice, opened to order. The list changes daily, so learn each name and where it grew.
cards.pairs: Mignonette, lemon, cocktail sauce, horseradish; Champagne, Chablis, Muscadet
cards.line: Half dozen oysters on the half shell, mignonette, lemon

cards.gist: Eggs of a female fish, cured loose or cooked whole in the sac
cards.guest: Roe is fish eggs. Salmon roe pops with a bright, salty burst, and spring shad roe is seared whole until it is creamy inside.
cards.why: Roe is the egg mass of a female fish, held in a thin sac. Loosened and salted, the eggs pop and taste of the sea: salmon roe is large and orange, flying fish roe tiny and crunchy. Cooked whole in the sac, like shad roe, it firms outside and turns creamy and grainy within.
cards.note: Loose salted roe, like salmon roe, is cured but never cooked: it is served raw.
cards.pairs: Blini, sour cream, chives, sushi rice, brown butter, bacon
cards.notThis: Caviar on its own means salted sturgeon roe. Any other roe sold as caviar has to name the fish, as in salmon caviar.
cards.line: Salmon roe, buckwheat blini, sour cream, chives
cards.prompt: __ is the egg mass of a female fish, held in a thin sac. Loosened and salted, the eggs pop and taste of the sea: salmon __ is large and orange, flying fish __ tiny and crunchy. Cooked whole in the sac, like shad __, it firms outside and turns creamy and grainy within.

cards.gist: Rich, oily pink fish that grows at sea and spawns back in rivers
cards.guest: Salmon is rich and buttery, with big, silky flakes. Wild king is the richest of all, and sockeye is leaner and deeper in flavor.
cards.why: Salmon hatch in rivers, fatten at sea and swim back upstream to spawn, so they carry fat for the trip. It keeps the flesh moist and gives it big, soft flakes. The color comes from a pigment in the krill and shrimp they eat. King is the fattiest species, sockeye the reddest.
cards.note: Often served medium, still translucent in the center. Guests can ask for it cooked through.
cards.origin: Wild from Alaska to California; Atlantic salmon on menus is almost always farmed
cards.notThis: Arctic char and trout look alike but are milder, with a finer flake. Steelhead is a sea-run trout that eats much like salmon.
cards.line: Seared king salmon, French lentils, beurre blanc

cards.gist: Sweet round muscle a shellfish uses to clap its two shells shut
cards.guest: Scallops are the sweet muscle that snaps the shell shut, seared golden on the outside and soft, almost creamy, in the middle.
cards.why: A scallop swims by clapping its shells, driven by one big muscle, and that muscle is what we eat. It is rich in glycogen and sweet amino acids, so it tastes sweet and browns well. Sea scallops are large and sear. Bay scallops are small and cook in seconds. Untreated dry ones sear best.
cards.note: Best seared golden and left just translucent in the center. Cooked through, they turn rubbery.
cards.notThis: Not king trumpet mushroom scallops, which are thick rounds of mushroom stem cut to look like the real thing.
cards.line: Seared sea scallops, cauliflower puree, brown butter

cards.gist: Red-skinned warm-reef fish, lean and sweet, often served whole
cards.guest: Snapper is a mild, slightly sweet white fish from warm Gulf waters. It is lean and flaky, and the skin crisps up beautifully.
cards.why: Snapper live on warm reefs in the Gulf of Mexico and the southern Atlantic. They are lean, so the flesh is mild and sweet with moist, medium flakes, and the red skin crisps well in a hot pan. Whole snapper, fried or grilled, is a classic of the Gulf and the Caribbean.
cards.note: Served whole, it arrives on the bone, with fins and small bones to work around.
cards.notThis: Not grouper, which is firmer and chunkier. West Coast Pacific snapper is usually rockfish, a different fish.
cards.line: Whole fried red snapper, green mango slaw, lime
cards.prompt: __ live on warm reefs in the Gulf of Mexico and the southern Atlantic. They are lean, so the flesh is mild and sweet with moist, medium flakes, and the red skin crisps well in a hot pan. Whole __, fried or grilled, is a classic of the Gulf and the Caribbean.

cards.gist: Ancient armored river fish, dense and meaty, prized for its eggs
cards.guest: Sturgeon is the fish caviar comes from. The meat is firm and rich, more like veal than a flaky fish, and it is wonderful smoked.
cards.why: Sturgeon have barely changed in 200 million years: rows of bony plates, not ordinary scales, and a skeleton mostly of cartilage. The flesh has almost no flake and a good amount of fat, so it eats dense and meaty, often compared to veal or lobster, and it takes smoke beautifully.
cards.origin: Mostly farmed white sturgeon from California and Idaho; wild stocks are protected
cards.pairs: Potato pancakes, sour cream, dill, horseradish, rye bread
cards.line: Smoked sturgeon, potato pancake, sour cream, dill

cards.gist: Lean deep-water fish that eats crab, sweet and firm like lobster
cards.guest: Tilefish is a lean white fish from deep Atlantic waters. It eats crab and shrimp, so it tastes sweet, a little like lobster, with firm, moist flakes.
cards.why: Golden tilefish live at the edge of the continental shelf, digging burrows in the clay and feeding on crabs and shrimp. That diet is why the flesh tastes so sweet, often compared to lobster or scallop. It is lean, with a firm, fine flake closer to halibut than to cod.
cards.origin: Deep Atlantic shelf edge, from New England down to the Gulf of Mexico
cards.line: Pan-roasted golden tilefish, clams, fennel broth

cards.gist: Mild, delicate freshwater fish, often pan-fried whole or split
cards.guest: Trout is a mild, delicate freshwater fish with tender flakes and thin skin that crisps in the pan. With brown butter and almonds, it is a classic.
cards.why: Most trout on menus is farmed rainbow trout, raised in cold spring water in places like Idaho. It is small and fairly lean, so the flesh is mild with fine, soft flakes and the skin is thin enough to eat crisp. Steelhead is rainbow trout that went to sea: bigger, richer and pinker.
cards.note: Served whole, it keeps its fine rib bones, and butterflied fillets can still hold a few small pin bones.
cards.notThis: Arctic char is a cousin with richer, pinker flesh. Salmon is bigger and much oilier.
cards.line: Pan-fried rainbow trout, brown butter, almonds

cards.gist: Prized European flatfish, firm and white, rich in gelatin at the bone
cards.guest: Turbot is one of the most prized fish in Europe, a flatfish with firm, snow-white flesh that is sweet and almost silky. It is often roasted whole.
cards.why: Turbot lie flat on the seabed, and their thick, muscular fillets eat firm and meaty rather than flaky. The skin and bones are rich in gelatin, which keeps the flesh moist and gives cooked turbot a silky, sticky richness that chefs pair with butter sauces.
cards.note: Often cooked on the bone to keep it juicy, so it may arrive whole or as a bone-in cut.
cards.origin: European coasts from Norway to the Mediterranean, much of it farmed in Spain
cards.notThis: Not halibut, a bigger, leaner flatfish. Cheap Greenland turbot is a different, softer and oilier fish.
cards.line: Whole roasted turbot for two, brown butter, potatoes

cards.gist: Deep-water Carolina fish that gathers at wrecks, with big flakes
cards.guest: It's a deep-water fish from off the Carolinas, firm and mild with big white flakes. It eats a lot like grouper.
cards.why: It lives far down on rocky ledges off South Carolina and Georgia, and got its name from gathering around shipwrecks. Caught by hook and line in a small fishery, it is lean with large, moist, sweet flakes, much like grouper or a big sea bass.
cards.origin: Southeast US, the deep Charleston Bump; named for hanging around wrecks
cards.notThis: Not grouper, though it eats like one. It is its own deep-water family and a local Carolina catch.
cards.line: Pan-roasted wreckfish, Carolina Gold rice, brown butter

cards.gist: Salt-cured sturgeon eggs, served cold by the small spoonful
cards.guest: It's sturgeon roe, lightly salted and served cold. Each pearl pops with a clean, briny, buttery flavor, best with a blini and a glass of Champagne.
cards.why: Eggs are taken from a sturgeon, screened, and lightly salted, which firms them and seasons them without cooking. Nearly all caviar today is farmed, since wild sturgeon were overfished and wild Caspian caviar is barely traded. Osetra, Kaluga and Siberian are common kinds.
cards.note: Served cold and never cooked. Kitchens often use a mother-of-pearl or bone spoon rather than metal.
cards.pairs: Blini, crème fraîche, chives, potato chips, Champagne or cold vodka
cards.notThis: Not just any fish eggs. On a US menu, salmon or trout eggs must name the fish, as in salmon caviar.
cards.line: Osetra caviar, buckwheat blini, crème fraîche, chives

cards.gist: Salted, pressed and dried fish-egg sac, grated like a cheese
cards.guest: It's cured fish roe, dried into an amber block and grated over the dish. Salty and savory, it tastes like the sea's answer to parmesan.
cards.why: The whole roe sac of a grey mullet or a tuna is salted, pressed and air-dried for weeks until firm and amber. Drying concentrates it into a salty, savory, faintly bitter seasoning. Mullet is milder and more delicate, tuna darker and stronger.
cards.note: Cured and dried, never cooked. It is shaved or grated over the dish at the end.
cards.origin: Italian, from Sardinia and Sicily; the word comes from Arabic
cards.pairs: Spaghetti, olive oil, lemon, garlic, toasted breadcrumbs
cards.line: Spaghetti, bottarga, lemon, garlic, breadcrumbs

cards.gist: Mild, lean Mediterranean white fish, often roasted and served whole
cards.guest: It's a Mediterranean sea bass, mild and delicate with crisp skin. It's often roasted whole with lemon and herbs, simple and light.
cards.why: The European sea bass, now mostly farmed in Greece and Turkey. Each fish is only a pound or two, so it suits one plate whole or as two fillets. The flesh is lean, white and finely flaked with a clean, sweet flavor, and the thin skin crisps well.
cards.note: Served whole, it comes with bones and head on. Many kitchens will fillet it before or at the table.
cards.origin: Italian name for the European sea bass; loup de mer in French
cards.notThis: Not black sea bass, the wild Atlantic fish. Branzino is the Mediterranean one, usually farmed.
cards.line: Whole roasted branzino, lemon, capers, herbs

cards.gist: Small wild Atlantic fish with firm, fine white flesh and crisp skin
cards.guest: It's a small wild fish from the Atlantic coast, sweet and delicate, and the skin crisps beautifully in the pan.
cards.why: A small grouper relative caught from New England to the Gulf by pot, hook and trawl. It stays small, a few pounds at most, so fillets are thin with a fine flake. The white flesh is sweet and mild, firmer than branzino, and the dark skin sears crisp.
cards.note: Thin fillets can hold a few fine pin bones.
cards.origin: US Atlantic coast, from Cape Cod down to Florida and the Gulf
cards.notThis: Not Chilean sea bass, a rich deep-water fish, and not branzino, the farmed Mediterranean one.
cards.line: Crispy-skin black sea bass, clams, fennel broth

cards.gist: Firm, buttery warm-water fish, often served raw, sturdy on a grill
cards.guest: Cobia is a firm, rich white fish from warm waters. It's buttery and clean served raw, and it holds up beautifully on the grill.
cards.why: A fast-swimming fish of warm seas, caught in the Gulf and farmed in open-ocean pens. It carries more fat than most white fish, so the meat is firm, moist and buttery with a clean, sweet flavor. Think somewhere between swordfish and snapper.
cards.note: Often served raw as crudo. Cooked, it stays moist even a little past medium.
cards.origin: Warm seas worldwide; Gulf anglers call it ling or lemonfish
cards.line: Cobia crudo, citrus, chili, olive oil

cards.gist: Big ocean hunter cut into thick, dense, mild steaks that grill well
cards.guest: Swordfish is meaty and mild, cut into thick steaks. It eats almost like a pork chop, great off the grill for someone who wants hearty fish.
cards.why: A large open-ocean fish, cut crosswise from the loin into boneless steaks. The flesh is dense with a tight grain and moderate fat, so it holds together on a grill and rarely breaks into flakes. It tastes mild, without the red-meat depth of tuna.
cards.note: The dark red band in each steak is the bloodline and is normal. Cooked past medium, it dries out fast.
cards.notThis: Not tuna, the other ocean steak. Swordfish is pale and cooked further, tuna deep red and served rare.
cards.line: Grilled swordfish, salsa verde, charred lemon

cards.gist: Deep-red, meaty ocean fish, served raw or seared rare inside
cards.guest: It's a meaty, deep-red fish, clean and rich. It's usually served raw, or seared outside and rare inside, closer to a steak than a flaky fish.
cards.why: Tuna are warm-bodied ocean sprinters, and their muscle is full of oxygen-carrying myoglobin, which makes it red and beefy. Yellowfin is lean, bigeye a little richer, and bluefin belly is marbled with fat. Albacore is the paler, milder one canned as white tuna.
cards.note: Usually served raw or rare. Cooked through, it firms up, dries and tastes like canned tuna.
cards.pairs: Soy, sesame, ginger, avocado, wasabi, citrus
cards.line: Seared ahi tuna, sesame, cucumber, ponzu

cards.gist: Dense, firm tail of a big-mouthed Atlantic fish, meaty and sweet
cards.guest: It's a firm, sweet white fish people call poor man's lobster. It holds together like a steak instead of flaking.
cards.why: Monkfish is an anglerfish, mostly head and mouth, so the tail is the main cut sold. That tail is dense, springy muscle around one central bone, with no flakes, so it eats sweet and meaty like shellfish and stands up to roasting, grilling and stews.
cards.note: A thin gray membrane is trimmed off first, or it shrinks and toughens in the pan.
cards.origin: North Atlantic anglerfish, sold as lotte on French menus
cards.line: Roasted monkfish, pancetta, white beans, salsa verde

cards.gist: Small ten-legged crustacean, sweet and snappy, sized by count
cards.guest: Sweet, firm shrimp, cooked just until they curl and turn pink, so they stay juicy with a little snap.
cards.why: Shrimp are ten-legged crustaceans, wild or farmed, from the Gulf to Asia. The meat is almost pure muscle protein that tightens fast in heat, so a minute too long turns it rubbery. Size is a count per pound: 16/20 means 16 to 20 shrimp, U-15 means under 15.
cards.note: The dark line down the back is the digestive tract. Kitchens usually pull it out, mostly for looks and grit.
cards.pairs: Garlic butter, grits, cocktail sauce, andouille, lemon
cards.line: Gulf shrimp and grits, tasso gravy, scallion

cards.gist: Chesapeake swimmer prized for sweet, hand-picked lump meat
cards.guest: It's the East Coast crab Maryland crab cakes are famous for. The meat is sweet and delicate, and the big jumbo lumps are the prize.
cards.why: A swimming crab of the Atlantic and Gulf with paddle-shaped back legs. The two big muscles driving those paddles give jumbo lump, the whitest, sweetest meat. Lump and backfin are smaller pieces, and claw meat is darker and stronger. Picking is slow handwork, hence the price.
cards.note: Hand-picked meat can hold small bits of shell and cartilage, even when picked carefully.
cards.origin: Atlantic and Gulf coasts, most famously Maryland's Chesapeake Bay
cards.pairs: Old Bay, drawn butter, crab cakes, remoulade, cold beer
cards.line: Jumbo lump blue crab cake, remoulade, charred lemon

cards.gist: Freshly molted Chesapeake swimmer, eaten whole with its legs
cards.guest: It's a blue crab caught just after it sheds its old shell, so you eat the whole thing. Crisp outside, sweet and juicy inside.
cards.why: Crabs grow by molting: they split the old shell and back out soft. Within hours the new one starts to firm, so watermen hold molting crabs in tanks and pull them the moment they emerge. The kitchen trims the face, gills and apron, then fries or sautés it whole.
cards.note: Eaten entirely, legs and all. The light crunch of the new shell is the point, not a mistake.
cards.origin: A late spring to summer delicacy, mostly from the Chesapeake Bay
cards.line: Fried soft-shell crab, remoulade, pickled green tomato

cards.gist: Big-clawed cold-water crustacean with a firm, sweet tail
cards.guest: It's the cold-water Atlantic kind with big claws. The tail is firm and sweet, the claw meat softer, and it all loves butter.
cards.why: A North Atlantic crustacean fished mostly off Maine and Canada. The tail is one big muscle, so it eats firm and snappy, while claws and knuckles are sweeter and softer. The meat breaks down fast after death, so it is cooked live or killed just before.
cards.note: The green paste in the body is tomalley, and dark beads in a female are roe, called coral, which turn red when cooked.
cards.notThis: Not spiny or rock lobster, a warm-water cousin with no big claws, usually sold as tails.
cards.line: Butter-poached Maine lobster, sweet corn, tarragon

cards.gist: Sand-burrowing two-shelled shellfish, briny and chewy
cards.guest: Clams are briny little shellfish with a pleasant chew. Small ones like littlenecks are eaten raw or steamed open in wine and garlic.
cards.why: Two-shelled animals that burrow in sand and mud and filter the water, so they taste of where they grew. Hard shells sell by size: littlenecks small and tender, cherrystones bigger, chowder clams biggest, tough and chopped. Soft-shell steamers have a neck skin to peel.
cards.note: Sold alive with shells shut. Littlenecks and cherrystones are often served raw on the half shell.
cards.notThis: Not mussels, which are longer, blue-black and smooth, and cling to rocks and ropes instead of burrowing.
cards.line: Linguine with littleneck clams, white wine, chili
